newsitem.title: USA: Wall St analysts upbeat on Chevron Tengiz.
newsitem.headline: Wall St analysts upbeat on Chevron Tengiz.

text.p: Wall Street analysts raised their expectations on Wednesday for Chevron Corp's earnings from the oil giant's joint venture in Kazakstan's Tengiz oilfield.

"In the fall, they told analysts they get would earn about $80 million. The meeting provided more specific financial details of the venture, and my personal belief is it's going to be more than that," said UBS Securities analyst Mark Gilman.
Chevron spokesman Mike Libbey confirmed earnings would be more than $80 million. But Libbey said exact profits would be announced in the company's 1996 annual report, due out in several weeks.

The revenues are dwarfed by Chevron's 1996 reported overall revenues of $42.8 billion, though it marks a significant profit increase for the $20 billion Tengiz oilfield project, in which Chevron currently owns a 50 percent stake.
The project, which analysts had for some time feared would prove a "white elephent", had been about break-even for Chevron in 1995.

Analysts who attended Wednesday's meeting expected most of the oilfield revenues to flow directly to net income due to a tax-loss carryforward and a minimal royalty payment to the Kazakstan government.

"Higher oil prices are flowing directly to the bottom line from the field," said Gilman of UBS, adding that royalties to Kazakstan will rise to 18 percent this April and Chevron's tax-loss carryforwards from the field will disappear in about three years.

Analysts said that by the end of 1996, Chevron had spent $800 million developing the fields, but estimated that the field's production costs dropped to about $4.15 a barrel in 1996, about half of what they were in 1995.

Chevron currently owns a 50 percent stake in the $20 billion Tengiz oilfield, located on the northeastern shores of Kazakstan's Caspian Sea. It's stake, however, will drop to 45 percent when a deal to sell five percent to Russia's Lukoil closes in a matter of weeks, Libbey said.
Mobil Corp and the Kazakstan government own the remaining interest in the field.
Daily production at the field climbed by 100,000 barrels-per-day (bpd) in 1996, Libbey said, attributing the increase to expanded shipping capacity and an increase in local oil customers.
"It trended up for the entire year, so that by December it was 160,000 bpd," Libbey said.
Daily production is expected to touch 185,000 bpd by the end of 1997, he said, with Chevron forecast to spend about $300 million to improve infrastructure at the field in 1997.
"This was a very positive meeting. The higher royalty in April will be offset by higher production," said Paul Ting, analyst with Salomon Brothers.
Chevron told analysts the field's pipeline will carry a tariff of $3.50 a barrel, and will be tied to U.S. inflation while being capped at $6.00 a barrel.
Chevron formed the joint venure with the Kazak government in 1993.
The longer-term success of Tengiz, located on the northeastern shores of Kazakstan's Caspian Sea, is dependent on the building of a pipeline extension to the Black Sea port of Novorossiisk.
The signing of the pipeline deal by the Caspian Pipeline Consortium in which Chevron owns a 15 percent stake is expected by March. Eight other oil companies own stakes in the pipeline.
